opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the really interesting things about ADHD is that it's a nice example of how what counts as a disorder depends a lot on the environment you're in. If you think about the explore-exploit tradeoff, which is something I've talked about a lot, children are designed to be explorers. They have broad, diffuse attention. They're paying attention to everything that's going on around them rather than focusing on one thing. They're more impulsive, more willing to try new things. And from an evolutionary perspective, that makes a great deal of sense, because childhood is this protected period where you can go out and learn about the world without having to worry about getting things done.

Now, what we call ADHD looks in many ways like a kind of extension of that exploratory, childlike style of attention. And there's variation. Some people are naturally more on the explore end and some more on the exploit end, and in a population that diversity is actually useful. You want some people who are noticing the unexpected thing in the corner, and some people who are focused on the task at hand.

The problem is that schooling, especially the kind of schooling that emerged in the last century or so, really demands a very particular kind of attention. Sit still, focus on this one thing for forty-five minutes, ignore everything else. That's a very unusual demand, historically. And it's not surprising that some children who would have been perfectly fine, maybe even advantaged, as hunters or foragers or apprentices learning by watching and doing, look like they have a problem in that setting.

There's a striking finding that the youngest children in a class are much more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD than the oldest children. Being born a few months later isn't giving you a neurological disorder. What it means is that we're comparing a child to a standard of focused attention that they're just developmentally not quite ready for yet.

I don't want to say that ADHD isn't real, or that there aren't people for whom it's genuinely debilitating, and for whom medication is enormously helpful. Stimulants essentially shift you toward the exploit end of the spectrum, and sometimes that's exactly what you need to get through the demands of modern life. But I think we should be careful about treating that as fixing a broken child, rather than recognizing that we've built an environment that rewards one kind of mind and penalizes another. The question is as much about how we design our institutions as it is about what's going on in an individual brain.

r001.rationale: The response describes children generally as having broad, diffuse attention, but does not refer to two-year-olds or specifically reframe their apparent inattention.

r002.rationale: It explains that schooling demands sustained, narrow focus and can make children with exploratory attentional styles appear to have a problem despite being suited to other environments.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the way to think about it is that there's a really wide range of variation in the way that children's attention works, and that variation has always been there. Attention isn't just one thing. There's the kind of attention that we usually mean when we talk about attention, which is the focused, top-down, executive kind, where you decide what's relevant and you screen out everything else. And then there's a more exploratory, broad, diffuse kind of attention, where you're taking in a lot of information from the environment without a particular goal in mind. If you look at young children, they're actually very good at that second kind of attention. In some of our studies, four-year-olds notice things that adults miss precisely because the adults have decided what's relevant and the children haven't.

So a lot of what looks like a deficit from one perspective looks like a feature from another. A child who has a lot of that exploratory attention is going to be very good at picking up on things in the environment, very good at being open to new possibilities, and not very good at sitting in a room for six hours and doing worksheets. Now, in an environment where children were out foraging, or learning by watching the adults around them, that profile might not have been a problem at all. It might even have been an advantage. What's happened is that we've constructed an environment, especially school, that puts an enormous premium on one particular kind of attention at a very young age, and then we're surprised that a lot of children don't fit.

I don't want to say that there aren't children who are genuinely struggling, or that there's nothing real there. There are children for whom the mismatch is severe enough that they're suffering, and we should help them. But I think it's a mistake to think of the variation itself as a pathology. It's more like the variation is a resource for the species, with some individuals who are focused and exploit what they already know, and others who are broad and explore. And then the question is whether the demands of the particular society we've built make room for both kinds of minds. And I'd say right now, we don't make much room for the explorers, especially when they're six.

r001.rationale: The response describes children’s broad, exploratory attention and gives an example involving four-year-olds, but it does not specifically reframe two-year-olds’ apparent inattention as attention spread across everything.

r002.rationale: The response says school places a strong premium on focused attention, causing some children not to fit, and distinguishes this societal mismatch from attentional variation itself being pathological.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish two questions. One is, how much variation is there in the way people attend to the world? And the other is, when does that variation become a source of difficulty or disability? Those aren’t quite the same question, because the second depends partly on what we’re asking people to do.

If you have an environment in which you’re supposed to sit still and concentrate on a task someone else has assigned for six hours, then being easily drawn to something new is going to be a disadvantage. In another environment, noticing what’s changed, exploring, moving from one possibility to another could be useful. There’s a trade-off between exploring new possibilities and exploiting the things you already know, and it makes sense that people would vary in how they manage that trade-off.

That doesn’t mean the difficulties associated with ADHD aren’t real, or that changing the classroom would make all of them disappear. People can have trouble doing things they themselves very much want to do. But we should be asking both how we can help the individual and whether we’ve made the demands of our institutions unnecessarily narrow. Especially with children, I’m wary of assuming that there’s one ideal way to pay attention and that every departure from it is a deficit.

r001.rationale: The response discusses variation in attention generally but does not reframe two-year-olds’ apparent inattention as attention spread across everything.

r002.rationale: It explains that demands to sit still and concentrate on assigned work can make exploratory attention a disadvantage, while that same variation may be useful in another environment; it also questions narrow classroom demands.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one useful way of thinking about ADHD is to distinguish between individual variation and the environments in which people find themselves. People vary in how readily they shift their attention, how much they explore, how much they’re drawn to something new rather than sticking with a particular task. And there can be advantages and disadvantages to either end of that spectrum.

If you’re in an environment where you have to sit still and concentrate on something that somebody else has decided you should concentrate on, then being very exploratory can be a real problem. In a different environment, noticing something unexpected and pursuing it might be exactly what you need.

That doesn’t mean that the difficulties associated with ADHD aren’t real, or that changing the classroom would make all of them disappear. But we should ask two questions: How can we help people who are struggling? And how much of that struggle comes from having organized our institutions around a fairly narrow range of human capacities? I think we’re much more accustomed to asking the first question than the second.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ADHD and exploratory attention, but does not mention two-year-olds or reframe their apparent inattention as attention spread across everything.

r002.rationale: It explains that settings requiring people to sit still and focus on assigned tasks can make exploratory attention a problem, while another environment may make it useful. It also points to classrooms and institutions organized around a narrow range of capacities.
